claims.text: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 can serve as a phosphorus-containing high-entropy-alloy baseline for forming an amorphous material by rapid cooling.
Introducing a modest amount of carbon into the phosphorus-containing HEA will improve its glass-forming ability.
Introducing carbon into the phosphorus-containing HEA will improve the thermal stability of its amorphous state.
Carbon improves glass formation and thermal stability by inhibiting crystallization during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure.
Melt spinning can provide cooling rates on the order of 10^5–10^6 K/s for the proposed alloy processing.
Effective integration of carbon into the alloy under rapid cooling is required for the proposed improvement.
Carbon will be localized at atomic interfaces or in minor carbon-rich regions within the amorphous matrix.
Localized carbon incorporation will disrupt long-range atomic ordering.
Carbon will reduce atomic mobility in the alloy.
Carbon-induced reduction of atomic mobility will increase the free-energy difference between the amorphous and crystalline states.
Short-range carbon bonds may hinder nucleation and growth of crystalline phases.
Carbon may create a protective carbon-enriched shell during rapid cooling that stabilizes the amorphous structure.
Carbon doping will increase the critical casting thickness or maximum castable diameter relative to an undoped, identically processed baseline.
Carbon doping will raise the DSC crystallization-onset temperature relative to the undoped baseline.
Carbon contents that are too high or too low may eliminate the beneficial effect.
Carbon segregation, oxidation, or ineffective incorporation may diminish the improvement.
Excessive or poorly incorporated carbon may adversely affect ductility.
The optimal carbon concentration and spatial distribution are not yet established.
